name: Beef tallow

lead: Beef tallow is beef fat rendered into a solid. It has long been used for frying, soap and candles, and has become popular in ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing communities as a cooking fat and as a moisturiser rubbed on the skin.

The chain is that as food it is a calorie-dense fat from a simple source, and on skin fats generally act as occlusives that slow water loss, leaving skin softer. Tallow is roughly 50 percent saturated and 42 percent monounsaturated fat. No published human trial was found testing it for skin or appearance, and Wikipedia describes some claims that it is healthier than seed oils as unscientific.

paras: People fry and roast with it in place of seed oils, and apply small amounts to the face as a balm, often at night. Users report on skin feel within days to weeks.

As food, tallow is high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and older diet studies found saturated fats raise serum cholesterol. Topical use has no published safety data, and moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some people.

social.title: Think twice before you smear beef tallow and salmon sperm on your face

chain: Used in cooking and on skin
angle.text: Beef tallow is used in ancestral-diet cooking and applied to the face as a moisturiser, aiming for softer, less dry-looking skin. As a fat it would be expected to hold moisture in; no trials have tested its skin effects.

lead: Tallow is rendered beef, pork or mutton fat, made mostly of triglycerides. Beef tallow is about 50 percent saturated fat, 42 percent monounsaturated and 4 percent polyunsaturated, with roughly 109 mg of cholesterol per 100 g [1]. It has long been used for frying, soap, candles and lubrication, and fast-food chains including McDonald's fried in tallow-based oil until around 1990 [1].

In recent years beef tallow has been promoted online as a healthier cooking fat than seed oils and as a skincare ingredient, a trend that has been associated with influencers and with US political figures [1]. Wikipedia describes some of these claims as unscientific [1].
No published human trial was found testing tallow, eaten or applied, for skin condition or appearance. Dietary research on tallow is mostly older work on serum cholesterol and animal studies.

paras: In industry, tallow refers to animal fat meeting technical criteria such as melting point, not only rendered suet, and in Britain rendered beef fat is called dripping. Main fatty acids are palmitic (about 25 percent), stearic (about 19 percent) and oleic (about 36 percent) [1].

Tallow has been used as a shortening and deep-frying fat and is an ingredient in pemmican. It is the main raw material for soap, producing sodium tallowate, and was long the standard material for molded candles [1]. It lubricated steam locomotives and ships into the 1950s, and tallow-derived fuel has been used in biodiesel blends [1].
Beef tallow was used for frying at several fast-food chains in the 1980s, and McDonald's used a tallow and cottonseed oil blend until 1990 [1].

Early controlled feeding work reported that serum cholesterol responses to saturated fat could be predicted by a formula, although the prediction failed for some fats, with discrepancies noted for beef tallow and cocoa butter [2]. Rodent studies have fed beef tallow as a high-fat control, for example one reporting greater body fat accumulation in rats on a beef tallow diet than on a safflower oil diet [3]. These are not studies of appearance.
Wikipedia notes that some influencers and US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have promoted tallow as healthier than seed oils and describes these claims as unscientific [1].

Proponents in ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing communities cook with tallow in place of seed oils and use it as a skin moisturiser, arguing that its fatty acid makeup resembles that of human skin oils. A separate entry covers skincare use. Moisturisers in general work in part by forming an occlusive layer that slows water loss from skin [4], but no study has tested tallow itself.

No studies found. No human trial was found testing beef tallow, eaten or applied topically, for skin or appearance. Related research consists of older studies of dietary saturated fat and serum cholesterol [2] and rodent diet studies [3].

lore.intro: In wellness and looksmaxxing circles, beef tallow is presented as a traditional, seed-oil-free fat for both eating and skin, though the evidence base for appearance effects is empty.

claims.claim: Tallow is healthier than seed oils for cooking.
Tallow on skin works as a moisturiser.

timeline.event: Concern over tallow or lard in rifle cartridge grease helps spark the Indian Mutiny [1].
A metabolic study reports how particular saturated fatty acids change serum cholesterol, with notes on beef tallow [2].
